disclosure: This section was drafted by Claude, a model made by Anthropic. Anthropic buys from, sells to or competes with companies named here, so read what it says about them with that in mind.

made_by.method: Research runs of one model read each vendor's own public pages (job listings, research posts, product pages and terms) and noted what each page shows the vendor being asked for or paid to do. A further run grouped the notes into signals and wrote each headline. Nothing was read from social media.
made_by.reviewed_by: separate reviewing runs of the same model checked every pairing of a vendor with a signal against that vendor's own note, withdrew the pairings no note supported and reworded headlines that claimed more than the notes show; no person reviewed each one

signals.headline: Vendors sell graders built to resist cheating, and audits that look for it
signals.implies: Rewards designed so a high score means the work was done, with graders attacked before delivery.

signals.headline: Vendors show a model improving on their data before they ask for an order
signals.implies: Evidence of uplift attached to each dataset, and trial terms that shift the risk to the seller.

signals.headline: Pass/fail is giving way to partial credit, rubrics and hybrid graders
signals.implies: Graders that score how far the agent got on decks, spreadsheets, legal work and long builds, not only whether it finished.

signals.headline: Many vendors name law among their professional domains
signals.implies: Legal environments, tasks and records alongside finance and medicine.

signals.headline: Expert judgement is bought to write rubrics, gold answers and calibrate judge models
signals.implies: Senior professional judgement converted into reusable scoring rules and judge-calibration sets.

signals.headline: Quality control increasingly pairs automated checks with expert auditors
signals.implies: Delivered data that has already been through independent checks and audit.

signals.headline: Vendors now capture skilled work in real workplaces as well as household chores
signals.implies: Footage of paid skilled work filmed where it happens, alongside household capture.

signals.headline: Coding tasks must be audited for leaked answers, broken tests and gameable graders
signals.implies: Coding tasks that arrive pre-audited, with scrubbed history and fair, deterministic graders.

signals.headline: Many vendors license data non-exclusively and keep the underlying asset
signals.implies: Vendors offer use-limited training rights rather than ownership, with paperwork attached.

signals.headline: Several robot builders pre-train on people's first-person video, some with no robot data at that stage
signals.implies: Human first-person video of manual tasks in very large volume, to pre-train robot models before any robot data is added.

signals.headline: Coding tasks now run for hours or days and rebuild whole programs
signals.implies: A steady supply of new, very long, product-scale software tasks the best model still fails.

signals.headline: Vendors now buy whole companies' internal records: chat, email, CRM, code, documents
signals.implies: Records of how real companies do work, across many industries, that are not on the public internet.

signals.headline: Buyers want test sets that no model has seen and none can game
signals.implies: Fresh, sealed evaluation data with contamination controls, often held and graded by a third party.

signals.headline: Vendors sell simulated companies: cloned work apps filled with files, chat and tasks
signals.implies: Whole-company practice worlds, in volume, organised by job and industry.

evidence.name: Haitian Ruisheng / Speechocean (北京海天瑞声, 688787)

signals.headline: Speech in under-served languages and dialects, Indic and Arabic singled out
signals.implies: Conversational audio and transcripts in dialects and languages beyond the few that commercial systems already speak.

signals.headline: Bought records are turned into practice environments, not handed to labs raw
signals.implies: Environments, tasks and verifiers built from real records, with the natural mess left in.

signals.headline: Non-exclusive licences are the default; the same data is sold to several buyers
signals.implies: Labs accept shared data and buy access or speed rather than ownership.

signals.headline: Pay is often per accepted task, with referral fees and paid training on top
signals.implies: Output-priced expert labour, and vendors paying to recruit scarce experts.

signals.headline: Robot operators are paid more by the hour than people who film at home
signals.implies: Robot-native demonstrations at US wages, plus cheap bulk first-person video.

signals.headline: Robot, video and audio buyers grade data on variety, spec and labels
signals.implies: Diverse, densely annotated, spec-compliant sensor data with metadata, not raw hours.

signals.headline: Builders split on buying versus collecting in-house, and on exclusivity
signals.implies: Some labs want outside collection at large weekly volumes; others want only the capture hardware, or nothing.

signals.headline: Capture is made to order and paid per accepted hour
signals.implies: Custom collection to each lab's schema, with acceptance thresholds and proof on the lab's own benchmarks.

signals.headline: Touch and force, recorded by gloves, are being added to video
signals.implies: Contact, force and finger-level motion time-locked to video, which cameras alone cannot give.

signals.headline: Private codebases with full history are the wanted raw material for coding
signals.implies: Never-public, team-built code with its history, to seed training tasks and clean tests.

signals.headline: Coding demand is spreading to kernels, infrastructure, migrations and scientific computing
signals.implies: Expert-built tasks in systems, performance and ML engineering, well beyond Python bug fixes.

signals.headline: Profession-specific private benchmarks are built from real records with practising experts
signals.implies: Evaluations in law, finance, tax, insurance, medicine and voice grounded in real working documents.

signals.headline: Benchmarks saturate fast, and testers keep replacing them with harder ones
signals.implies: New expert-built tests that still separate the top models, refreshed as each one is passed.

signals.headline: Senior lawyers, bankers and doctors are offered some of the highest hourly rates
signals.implies: Small volumes of top professional judgement, turned into tasks, rubrics and graded answers.

signals.headline: Tasks are tuned to a pass-rate band on current models
signals.implies: Hard-but-solvable tasks delivered with measured pass rates, and re-measured as models improve.

signals.headline: The unit sold is a task with its grader, not a bare environment
signals.implies: Ready-to-run task packages that drop into the lab's training harness and score deterministically.

signals.headline: Vendors and testers build software tasks that take an agent hours, days or a week
signals.implies: Very long, exactly graded software projects, and training set-ups for orchestrator-plus-sub-agent work.

signals.headline: Vendors publish website terms but not their lab contracts; one says fees sit in separate order forms
signals.implies: Custom paperwork per deal: data rights, usage limits, service levels and publicity rights.

signals.headline: Video is delivered with step labels, hand pose and recovered geometry
signals.implies: Time-stamped action text, hand and body pose and scene geometry delivered ready to train on, not raw footage.

signals.headline: Testers measure what agents do unprompted: lying, collusion, overstepping, self-modification
signals.implies: Propensity tests in realistic deployments, plus monitors and environments built with lab safety teams.

signals.headline: AI research itself is a named science target: agents doing ML engineering
signals.implies: Open-ended ML-research tasks with hidden tests, scored against human records.

signals.headline: Sellers of first-person and robot data name world-model builders as customers alongside robot labs
signals.implies: First-person video, robot logs and scans of places with physical properties, sold once to robot and world-model teams alike.

signals.headline: Labs hand unreleased models to outside testers for scores to publish at launch
signals.implies: Independent, fast, confidential assessment timed to release, credible to customers and regulators.

signals.headline: Accounting back-office work is a named target: closing the books and reconciliation
signals.implies: Tasks that must be right every time, inside accounting systems.

signals.headline: Finance experts are hired to write problems and rubrics and to grade output
signals.implies: Practitioners with finance credentials producing ground truth.

signals.headline: Vendors are adding insurance, credit, tax and compliance work alongside investment banking
signals.implies: The same task-and-rubric data for neighbouring financial professions.

signals.headline: Vendors sell tasks in fields where a tool, not a person, settles correctness
signals.implies: Tasks in maths, chips, cyber, science and data science whose rewards come from running a checker.

signals.headline: Tasks, harnesses and delivery are converging on shared formats
signals.implies: Deliverables that plug into the lab's existing harness, evaluation framework and data loaders.

signals.headline: Finding and vetting experts fast is treated as a product in itself
signals.implies: Vetted specialists on demand, matched to whatever labs want this month.

signals.headline: A long tail of narrow jobs: trades, inspection, defence, design, language
signals.implies: Practical know-how and specialist media that sit outside the big professional domains.

signals.headline: Payment follows acceptance; rejected hours, clips and files earn nothing
signals.implies: Buyers pay for verified quality and push reject risk down to suppliers and workers.

signals.headline: Sellers publish benchmark gains from their data on open models
signals.implies: Data aimed at the tests that rankings weight most, with transfer to tests the seller did not write.

signals.headline: Variety, rare cases and failures are valued above more hours
signals.implies: Coverage of many tasks, objects, tools and places, plus mistakes and recoveries, rather than repeats of one scene.

signals.headline: PhD-level contributors are recruited across many fields and countries
signals.implies: Vetted graduate scientists for problem writing, review and audit.

signals.headline: Environments and tasks are increasingly generated by software, not hand-built
signals.implies: Large numbers of machine-made environments, with automated checks on their quality.

signals.headline: Testers and vendors now grade whether code is mergeable, not only whether tests pass
signals.implies: Preference data, rubrics and rewards that capture engineering judgement and reliability, not only correctness.

signals.headline: Company data is de-identified and rights-checked before use; one licence also bars scraped and machine-made content
signals.implies: Training-safe records: personal details removed, rights confirmed, and in some cases the source company hidden.

signals.headline: Vendors are hiring people whose whole job is buying data from companies
signals.implies: A standing supply of licensed private company data, sourced by the vendor on labs' behalf.

signals.headline: Evaluation is sold as the front end of a data sale
signals.implies: A vendor that measures the gap, then sells the tasks that close it.

signals.headline: Testers are paid to measure dangerous abilities and bad behaviour, not just skill
signals.implies: Independent risk and propensity scores alongside capability scores, including AI-research acceleration.

signals.headline: Software engineers are paid by the hour, or per task, to build coding tasks
signals.implies: Production-experienced engineers writing, reviewing and auditing agent coding tasks.

signals.headline: Banking and private-equity deliverables recur across vendors: models, decks, diligence
signals.implies: End-to-end deal work product in real file formats.

signals.headline: Sensitive buyers want training to happen where the data already sits
signals.implies: Train-in-place access and on-premises delivery in place of file transfer.

signals.headline: Training and evaluation need very many isolated sandboxes at once
signals.implies: Cheap, isolated, production-like execution environments at reinforcement-learning volume.

signals.headline: Practising lawyers are paid to write legal tasks with case files and grading criteria
signals.implies: Expert-written legal assignments, reviews of AI work product, and negotiated contract edits.

signals.headline: Day-long AI-research tasks are built to measure models improving models
signals.implies: Environments and evaluations for agents doing AI research, with graders that cannot be passed without doing the work.

signals.headline: Vendors sell replicas of named work apps for agents to act in
signals.implies: Frozen, faithful copies of real software, because live sites change and block bots.

signals.headline: Vendors recruit and collect for specialist tools such as CAD, chip-design, energy and spreadsheet software
signals.implies: People who can demonstrate and grade work inside specific professional applications.

signals.headline: Labs arrive with vague goals and expect the vendor to shape the data fast
signals.implies: Research-partner relationships with the post-training team, delivered in days.

signals.headline: Data is ordered to fit a named training method, including agent-recovery examples
signals.implies: Demonstrations, preference data, reward data and environments, each to specification.

signals.headline: Robot and biology builders publish scaling results that justify buying more data
signals.implies: More hours and more varied data, with human video and licensed footage as proven supplements.

signals.headline: Test and training environments are themselves being attacked by the models
signals.implies: Sandboxes and graders proven to contain a model that is actively trying to get out or cheat.

signals.headline: Vendors count coding environments by the task and quote costs per task
signals.implies: Coding environments built by senior engineers, with cost tracked per task.

signals.headline: The record of how work happened is worth more than the finished product
signals.implies: Linked, time-ordered records showing decisions and reasoning, not only outcomes.

signals.headline: Enterprises are sold small specialist models that are cheaper and faster
signals.implies: Data, environments and training runs that make an open model good at one company's job.

signals.headline: Generalist work, and work outside the United States, is still listed at far lower rates
signals.implies: Bulk evaluation and non-English coverage, bought cheaply.

signals.headline: Scientists and engineers with doctorates are paid by the hour
signals.implies: Graduate-level problems, formal proofs and engineering judgement, at lower rates than law or finance.

signals.headline: Vendors pay their own task builders and researchers lab-level salaries
signals.implies: Environment and benchmark design by senior researchers, not contractors.

signals.headline: Game footage is sold with the player's keyboard, mouse or controller inputs
signals.implies: Video time-locked to the inputs that produced it, in bulk, for world models and game-playing agents.

signals.headline: Real doctor-patient conversations and dictation are a named audio category
signals.implies: Real clinical speech with checked transcripts, where drug and lab terms must survive.

signals.headline: Practising clinicians are paid to write hard cases and grade model reasoning
signals.implies: Clinical scenarios, multi-rater ground truth and corrected step-by-step reasoning.

signals.headline: Buyers want the same patient over time, across scans, notes, labs and genomics
signals.implies: Linked, de-identified records broad enough for general medical models.

signals.headline: Logs of live agents, especially humans correcting them, are treated as prime training data
signals.implies: Correction events and tool-use sessions from real deployments, turned into environments.

signals.headline: Incidents show evaluation and training environments need to be sealed and tamper-resistant
signals.implies: Network-isolated sandboxes, tamper-resistant logging and security review of test set-ups.

signals.headline: Task length and difficulty must keep rising as models improve
signals.implies: Each model generation needs a new, longer and harder set; last year's tasks lose value.

signals.headline: Screen recordings with aligned mouse and keyboard events are a purchased input
signals.implies: Long expert workflows in real software, with inputs, reasoning and a checkable result.

signals.headline: The wanted task is files in, a finished deliverable out, scored by rubric
signals.implies: Spreadsheets, slide decks and memos as gradable outputs.

signals.headline: Some vendors organise coverage by occupation across many sectors of the economy
signals.implies: Breadth: tasks for ordinary operational jobs, not only elite professions.

signals.headline: Buyers often sample or pilot first, and some vendors describe orders arriving in bursts
signals.implies: Try-before-buy samples, agreed acceptance tests, and campaign-style purchasing.

signals.headline: Production code is bought with its commits, reviews and tickets, not as snapshots
signals.implies: Unflattened private repositories with the surrounding paper trail.

signals.headline: Vendors sell diagnosis: find where the model fails, then supply the fix
signals.implies: A supplier that names the model's gap and proves the remedy against the lab's own numbers.

signals.headline: Robot builders and vendors feed data from deployed robots back into training
signals.implies: Data from robots at work, obtained through deployment and partnership.

signals.headline: Builders run teleoperation in-house with hourly operators, in one case around the clock
signals.implies: Trained operators and robot uptime are the constraint; labs staff this themselves or pay a vendor to.

signals.headline: Some builders report needing only minutes to hours of robot data per new task
signals.implies: Small, exact sets of robot demonstrations for the last training step, not bulk teleoperation as a base.

signals.headline: Cyber is becoming a training domain, with exploit-or-patch as the reward
signals.implies: Security tasks, environments and practitioner labour for training models to find and fix vulnerabilities.

signals.headline: Licensed, rights-cleared video is bought, with brokers holding exclusive AI rights
signals.implies: Training-only licences with clear provenance, bought through whichever broker holds the catalogue.

signals.headline: Orders have shifted from bulk libraries to narrow, curated, commissioned clips
signals.implies: Scene-level clips chosen or shot for one model objective, delivered fast and repeatedly.

signals.headline: Private speech test sets and human ratings of voice models are being built and offered
signals.implies: Unseen conversational test data and paid human judgement of naturalness, empathy and timing.

signals.headline: Real speech from named settings: clinics, call centres, courtrooms
signals.implies: Domain dialogue for voice agents in customer service and medicine, with transcripts.

evidence.name: Haitian Ruisheng / Speechocean (北京海天瑞声, 688787)

signals.headline: Natural two-way conversation with each speaker on a separate channel
signals.implies: Unscripted, wide-band, channel-separated dialogue with overlap kept, for speech-to-speech models.

signals.headline: GPU and custom-accelerator kernel writing is a sold task type
signals.implies: Performance-engineering tasks scored against a measured reference on named hardware.

signals.headline: Recorded sessions of developers working with coding agents are bought as data
signals.implies: Real developer-and-agent trajectories, with expert preferences, for imitation and preference training.

signals.headline: Coding data is sold with a measured gain on someone else's benchmark
signals.implies: Evidence, on an open model and an outside test, that a coding set moves scores before the lab buys.

signals.headline: Some vendors publish what they will pay for one company's records
signals.implies: Published ranges rise for long, rare, proprietary operating histories; referral bounties are offered for finding sellers.

signals.headline: Sourcing works backwards from what labs ask for; one vendor says it can start within days
signals.implies: Labs issue written data requirements; vendors find the holders and sign them.

signals.headline: Drug makers license biological and clinical data to train their own models
signals.implies: Licensed patient, perturbation and assay data as training input for in-house models.

signals.headline: One vendor says it built finance environments with most leading closed labs; others sell finance environments to labs
signals.implies: Long-horizon financial reasoning environments whose rewards need scarce domain experts.

signals.headline: Public finance tests are saturating; vendors sell harder tasks with partial-credit grading
signals.implies: Process-level rewards and tasks an agent cannot score on with a fake deliverable.

signals.headline: Vendors screen contributor work to show it was really made by a human
signals.implies: Provenance checks: screening for machine-written content and automated submissions.

signals.headline: Independent evaluation on real patient records is becoming a product of its own
signals.implies: A third party that holds real clinical test data and does the grading.

signals.headline: Video and robot builders are sizing pipelines for very large volumes of footage
signals.implies: Intake, storage and capture capacity for very large volumes of video and robot data.

signals.headline: Run logs are too large to read, so trace tooling is being built
signals.implies: Tools that turn huge volumes of agent transcripts and raw data into findings.

signals.headline: Some data and environment vendors now run post-training on substantial compute of their own
signals.implies: Suppliers that can train on their own environments and host a customer's training run.

signals.headline: Vendors publish long professional assignments with real deliverables that take a person many hours
signals.implies: Whole-job, under-specified professional tasks as tests and possible training material.

signals.headline: Vendors claim small sets of expert tasks lift scores on professional tests
signals.implies: Small, expensive, expert-built task sets that transfer across domains.

evidence.name: Haitian Ruisheng / Speechocean (北京海天瑞声, 688787)

signals.headline: The buyer set is widening to Chinese, state and open-model builders
signals.implies: Launch-driven, custom data for a broader set of model builders.

signals.headline: Vendors say environment supply, not lab budget, is the constraint
signals.implies: A continuing supply of new, harder environments, mainly for training.

signals.headline: Consent records, licence trails and security certificates are now a gate to deals
signals.implies: Documented, human-origin, lawfully licensed data from suppliers who pass audit.

signals.headline: One vendor sells training by the token; several report that a single evaluation run is costly
signals.implies: Budgets for many repeats of expensive runs, with cost per task tracked beside score.

signals.headline: Environments are priced per task
signals.implies: Complete, gradable tasks bought by the unit.

signals.headline: Rarity and length of history set the price of a company's records
signals.implies: Old, proprietary, hard-to-find domains rather than bulk volume.

signals.headline: Robot and first-person video data is often priced by the hour
signals.implies: Hourly rates vary with content value and volume.

signals.headline: Small sets of expert-built tasks are presented as enough
signals.implies: A small number of hard, expert-built tasks in each field, in place of mass labelling.

signals.headline: One seller gives away plain factory video; top buyers ask for depth, stereo and a higher frame rate
signals.implies: Synchronised stereo, depth, motion-sensor and wrist-camera capture with calibration; plain single-camera video has little price left.

signals.headline: Failed, sloppy and autonomous robot runs are kept as training data
signals.implies: Robot data across quality levels, labelled as success or failure, including human take-overs when a robot fails.

signals.headline: Testers and vendors are hardening security to hold models and data
signals.implies: Suppliers with hardened systems and tighter access controls.

signals.headline: Red-team labour is hired by risk area, credential and language
signals.implies: Adversarial prompts, refusal-boundary sets and policy grading from credentialed specialists, in many languages.

signals.headline: Machine-checked proofs are wanted; one vendor says the appeal is a grader that cannot be fooled
signals.implies: Formal proofs and statement-matching checks, usable directly as a reward signal.

signals.headline: Vendors are measuring synthetic data's effect, and one data licence forbids it outright
signals.implies: Synthetic data used where its benefit is tested, and kept out of some human-origin sets.

signals.headline: Robot-model builders lean on simulation and generated video, mixed with real data
signals.implies: Physically accurate simulation assets and generated video to stretch scarce real robot data.

signals.headline: Synchronised multi-camera footage and raw-versus-edited pairs sell as their own products
signals.implies: Paired before/after video and time-locked multiple views of one action, to teach editing and cutting between angles.

signals.headline: Vendors say video buyers want native high resolution, recent footage, steady cameras and high frame rates
signals.implies: True high-resolution, high-dynamic-range source footage with camera metadata, not up-scaled or graded archive material.

signals.headline: Vendors offer world-model builders video joined to the inputs that caused it
signals.implies: Footage paired frame by frame with inputs and scene state, so a model can learn what follows an action.

signals.headline: Speech is collected to order with consent records; one vendor licenses non-exclusively by default
signals.implies: Capability-targeted collections with per-clip provenance; some datasets are sold to more than one buyer.

evidence.name: Haitian Ruisheng / Speechocean (北京海天瑞声, 688787)

signals.headline: Transcripts must be verbatim, tightly timed, and mark noises and overlap
signals.implies: Human-checked, word-for-word transcripts with speaker turns, timing and non-speech events.

signals.headline: Vendors are starting to collect and list face and voice recorded together
signals.implies: Synchronised face, gesture and voice for models that see and talk.

signals.headline: Two lab-data vendors say AI buyers want clean, well-documented data, ordered in campaigns
signals.implies: Low-noise, standardised results with failures kept, returned quickly enough for model-in-the-loop work.

signals.headline: Vendors are adding primary cells, organoids and animal models alongside cell lines
signals.implies: Perturbation data from samples nearer to patients, with readouts over time.

signals.headline: Labs and datasets are pitched as ways to check general models' hypotheses
signals.implies: Physical validation of model predictions, and lab data organised as environments and evaluations for science agents.

signals.headline: Drug makers and institutes commission single-cell perturbation data built for model training
signals.implies: Interventional data — many drugs or gene edits, measured cell by cell under one protocol — rather than observational leftovers.

signals.headline: Some enterprises train on their own production traces rather than sell them
signals.implies: Enterprises want training on logs, corrections and QA labels that never leave their control.

signals.headline: Deals come as one-off file exports or as continuing collection
signals.implies: Both one-off exports and recurring supply are offered; some vendors seek recurring agreements.

signals.headline: The buyers' own job posts say this market has no settled price
signals.implies: Deal structures and prices for private data are being invented now, with several buyers bidding.

signals.headline: Healthcare and finance data are bought direct from the institutions holding them
signals.implies: Licensed sector datasets with compliance and data-rights terms attached.

signals.headline: Vendors say enterprise customers often need help deciding what to train and how to score it
signals.implies: Scoping, success criteria and trusted graders supplied along with the training.

signals.headline: Companies want to train on their own data without giving it to a lab
signals.implies: Post-training that leaves data, traces and weights under the customer's control.

signals.headline: The customer's own traces, workflows and evals become the training material
signals.implies: Pipelines that convert a company's live usage into tasks, graders and training signal.

signals.headline: Evaluation runs now cost real money, and human baselines are often missing
signals.implies: Funded compute and expert human baselines for serious evaluation.

signals.headline: Vendors sell private tests to help enterprises choose models and judge agent readiness
signals.implies: Evidence on the buyer's own work, not public scores, before large model or agent spending.

signals.headline: Brokers take exclusive AI rights from owners, then license non-exclusively to labs
signals.implies: Rights-cleared media with one seller per catalogue, so labs must come through the broker.

signals.headline: One robot-data vendor reports buyers moving to a single supplier; another vendor offers isolated collection per customer
signals.implies: Consistent data from a single source, collected in a set-up no other customer shares.

signals.headline: Biology data funders and contributors get a timed head start, not permanent exclusivity
signals.implies: Early access for those who pay or contribute, then wider release.

signals.headline: Voice actors and rare-language transcribers are listed at higher rates than ordinary speakers
signals.implies: Performed emotion and scarce languages; plain conversation is cheap.

signals.headline: Real financial paperwork is bought as raw material, from firms and individuals
signals.implies: Authentic, de-identified financial records to seed tasks and environments.

signals.headline: Games are used as long-running test and training environments for agents
signals.implies: Very long sequential-decision tasks with a built-in score, used to test and train agents.

signals.headline: Healthcare back-office work is wanted: billing codes, scheduling and operations
signals.implies: Medical coding and operations data; models score much higher on clinical notes than on billing codes.

signals.headline: A lab buys recordings of developers coding with AI assistants on their own projects, and another vendor pays developers for the same
signals.implies: Real developer-agent sessions with step-by-step expert preferences.

signals.headline: Long agent runs need snapshot, resume and a durable record of every run
signals.implies: Stateful environments that can be saved, branched, replayed and audited after the fact.

signals.headline: Courtroom audio appears as a named legal data category
signals.implies: Legal speech data beyond contract and case documents.

signals.headline: Legal benchmarks are private, built from real matters, with long documents and dense rubrics
signals.implies: Large held-out legal test sets that separate model faults from product faults.

signals.headline: Testers measure whether agents stay coherent and honest over very long runs
signals.implies: Long-running, adversarial tests of sustained judgement, plus data on recovery from mistakes.

signals.headline: Long tasks need feedback along the way, not one score at the end
signals.implies: Dense, localised reward signals and new scoring methods for long, real-world work.

signals.headline: Long runs need pause, resume, checkpoint and replay built into the environment
signals.implies: Environments that survive day-long runs and can be stopped, inspected, branched and replayed.

signals.headline: Tool-use environments expose very many callable tools
signals.implies: Multi-step API tasks with checkable end states, across terminal, browser and business tools.

signals.headline: Harder office tasks are long, vague and buried in noise, and models still fail
signals.implies: Tasks that need the agent to work out the job, in messy context, over hours or days.

signals.headline: Step-by-step records of people doing office work are a listed product
signals.implies: Authentic traces of routine work, including mundane hand-offs between co-workers.

signals.headline: Some health and biology data vendors sell governed access rather than downloadable files
signals.implies: Buyers may train where the data sits and cannot always take raw files away.

signals.headline: Some content licensors are testing pay-per-use terms; one says recent content is worth more
signals.implies: Usage reported by the buyer under standard terms, with recent content possibly priced higher.

signals.headline: Private code is wanted because public code no longer gives a clean measurement
signals.implies: Unseen codebases as the basis for honest coding scores and hard training tasks.

signals.headline: Buyers want a forecast of what an environment will teach before spending compute
signals.implies: A reliable per-environment estimate of training value, so compute is not wasted on tasks that teach nothing.

signals.headline: Some data vendors now sell post-training and a working robot, not only datasets
signals.implies: A robot post-trained for one job on the customer site, with data collected as part of the service.

signals.headline: Some sellers offer teleoperation on the buyer's own robot; one calls it its most valuable tier
signals.implies: Demonstrations on the exact robot to be deployed, with force and motion, run by someone else.

signals.headline: One world-model builder is collecting real robot logs; one free set has been used as a test set
signals.implies: Real robot logs to ground simulators, and neutral test sets; one robot maker gives its data away.

signals.headline: Science and engineering tasks are built around simulations and recomputable answers
signals.implies: Tasks in physics, chemistry, biology and engineering whose results a script can check.

signals.headline: Demonstrations can come from a stronger model instead of from people
signals.implies: In some cases vendors supply tasks and graders while a strong model supplies the trajectories.

signals.headline: Stand-in data lets some firms train without exposing customer records
signals.implies: Stand-in or synthetically rewritten versions of confidential workloads.

signals.headline: Video must arrive labelled: captions, camera moves, pose and action boundaries
signals.implies: Per-clip labels for action, subject, camera motion and timing, tightly aligned to the footage.

signals.headline: Acted, emotional speech and fine-grained emotion labels are in demand; one marketplace pays voice actors most
signals.implies: Performed speech labelled by emotion and tone, to make synthetic voices expressive.

signals.headline: One expert-labour vendor publishes a biology lab-image benchmark
signals.implies: Hard, expert-written biology questions and working lab images, not textbook figures.

signals.headline: Gene-sequence data from outside public databases, collected under benefit-sharing agreements
signals.implies: Diverse, long-read sequence data with documented consent, as fuel for biological foundation models.

signals.headline: One vendor licenses patient images and sequencing data for buyers to train their own models
signals.implies: Multimodal clinical data on the same patients over time, licensed for model training.

signals.headline: Drug companies pool standardised antibody measurements while keeping sequences private
signals.implies: Purpose-designed, standardised protein measurements, with training rights on others' data but not the raw files.

signals.headline: Labs pay a small specialist for chip-design environments
signals.implies: Chip-design tasks graded by real tool feedback, up to a manufacturable design.

signals.headline: One vendor hires hardware engineers and semiconductor experts for judgement on real builds
signals.implies: Expert data from people who designed, built and debugged physical products.

signals.headline: One chip-design vendor says labs give it unreleased models and work with it frequently
signals.implies: Private, per-model capability reports on hardware tasks, and joint work rather than a catalogue sale.

signals.headline: One robot-data unit weighs sourcing through a marketplace as well as in-house
signals.implies: More robot data than in-house collection can supply, pulled from partners.

signals.headline: One tester sells enterprises private benchmarks to guide which model they pay for
signals.implies: Proof on the buyer's own work of which model or agent is reliable enough.

signals.headline: Exclusivity is available at several times the price
signals.implies: A minority of buyers will pay a large premium to keep a task set or dataset to themselves.

signals.headline: One vendor makes sellers warrant the data has not been licensed this way before
signals.implies: First use: the seller warrants no earlier grant of the same rights.

signals.headline: One vendor lists safety red-teamers and policy graders as their own paid line
signals.implies: Specialist judgement on whether model outputs are dangerous, in many languages.

signals.headline: One forecasting firm says hard questions are the scarce input and pays for them
signals.implies: Questions in the band between solved and unknowable, answered with reasoning.

signals.headline: Three large labs fund a live forecasting benchmark; one invested in a forecasting firm
signals.implies: Questions whose answers are not yet known, so they cannot be memorised.

signals.headline: A staffing vendor lists work writing analyst forecasts from a fixed evidence cutoff
signals.implies: Point-in-time reports on markets, elections and drug launches, in the source language.

signals.headline: One vendor records long, scripted play sessions to cover rare events
signals.implies: Directed capture of unusual behaviour and long temporal context, which uploaded highlight clips lack.

signals.headline: One vendor sells engine-level ground truth with the footage: depth, camera pose, physics
signals.implies: Measured, not estimated, scene state alongside each frame, for labs without their own game studios.

signals.headline: A vendor claiming the largest action-labelled game corpus pitches transfer to robots
signals.implies: Action-labelled play as a base for agents that act in the physical world; whether outside labs will pay for it is not shown.

signals.headline: One vendor licenses game data at per-hour rates with provenance records, player consent and evaluation-only samples
signals.implies: Auditable rights for training, with try-before-buy and optional exclusivity.

signals.headline: One clinical-data company says drug makers license its patient data to train models, and one bought the model
signals.implies: Outcome-linked data that predicts which patients respond to a drug.

signals.headline: An arena tests unreleased models on real users and shares feedback with model developers
signals.implies: De-identified real prompts, votes and full agent sessions, plus independent behaviour counts.

signals.headline: One vendor is hiring a legal operations lead for data-licence paperwork
signals.implies: Recurring data-rights and usage terms across vendor agreements.

signals.headline: One vendor built a synthetic stand-in from public legal documents because client data could not be used
signals.implies: Cheaper specialised models for document review, trained without touching client files.

signals.headline: Vendors test assistants on real phones and build replicas of consumer apps and sites
signals.implies: In-market, on-device evaluation and phone-app environments.

signals.headline: One vendor says labs build the interface themselves and buy the domain work
signals.implies: Deterministic, cheat-resistant checks and tasks tuned just beyond current models.

signals.headline: AI companies are said to pay for fresh, structured web content over crawling
signals.implies: Clean, de-duplicated, real-time feeds with freshness and quality signals.

signals.headline: One evaluator tests agents running real businesses and reports cost per run
signals.implies: Side-by-side real-world comparisons and human cost baselines.

signals.headline: Contributor terms at several vendors assign all rights in the work to the vendor
signals.implies: Clean ownership of the work with no residual claims from contributors.

signals.headline: Repositories are converted into graded tasks, sometimes for one customer's own model
signals.implies: Issue-to-fix task sets with tests, cut from private repositories.

signals.headline: Code reaches buyers through dead start-ups, non-exclusive licences and cleared rights
signals.implies: Rights-cleared private code under non-exclusive licence, sourced from companies that no longer need it.

signals.headline: Simulated environments must show they transfer to the real product
signals.implies: Simulators with measured transfer, in many varieties, paired with practice on real sites.

signals.headline: A few vendors run tests of robot models on real hardware
signals.implies: Scoring of robot models on physical robots.

signals.headline: Where a price is shown, real-robot teleoperation data is priced above robot data overall
signals.implies: Reported prices are highest for real-robot demonstrations; published rates are rare.

signals.headline: One outside tester is let inside labs for audits and incident investigations
signals.implies: Trusted third parties with deep access who can audit internal agent use and investigate incidents.

signals.headline: One cyber tester says labs buy its offensive-cyber tests before releases
signals.implies: Fresh, private, realistic attack scenarios scored on the raw model within the release window.

signals.headline: Labs commission and own research-level maths problems, audits and verifiers
signals.implies: Problems past expert level with checkable answers, plus third-party scoring.

signals.headline: People are paid to rank and fault-find generated video
signals.implies: Human preference and defect labels on generated video.

signals.headline: Contributor work sessions are themselves instrumented and recorded
signals.implies: Screen-recorded, in-market use of an assistant, with session telemetry kept as data.

signals.headline: Weak-evidence sellers say price follows rarity, rigour and age, not size
signals.implies: Scarce-language, well-tested, human-era code from complex products.

themes.proof_of_lift: Proof that the data improves a model

vendors.name: 1X
vendors.sells: Robot-model builder. Trains on web video, human first-person video and a smaller amount of robot data; operators at its own site and customers' robots; a named outlet reports a data vendor as a supplier.

vendors.name: AfterQuery
vendors.sells: Training and test data made with paid professionals: worked examples with reasoning, grading rubrics, tool-using and computer-using environments, ready-made datasets, custom benchmarks. For enterprises, custom model training and on-site engineers.

vendors.name: Andon Labs
vendors.sells: Tests of whether an AI agent can run something alone for a long time, and how it behaves: simulated businesses and real ones run by an agent.

vendors.name: Appen
vendors.sells: People-made data for training and testing AI: alignment feedback, agentic and coding data, RL environments, speech and multimodal, physical-AI data, model evaluation, research services and an off-the-shelf catalog. Appen China serves Chinese model builders; Appen Global serves US hyperscalers and labs.

vendors.name: Applied Compute
vendors.sells: A platform to train open-weight models with reinforcement learning on the customer's own data and graders, serve them and keep training on production traffic; sold with researchers placed inside the customer.

vendors.name: Apptronik
vendors.sells: Robot-model builder. Collects humanoid data that feeds Google DeepMind's robotics models, at its own site and at customers' sites.

vendors.name: Basecamp Research
vendors.sells: Drug candidates and design work from its own biology models, through pharma partnerships. It keeps its private gene-sequence dataset; no page offers the raw data for licence.

vendors.name: Bespoke Labs
vendors.sells: RL environments built to look like a whole company (large codebase, microservices, tickets, chat, logs), the platform that generates and runs them, and agent optimization including post-training small open models for enterprises.

vendors.name: Build AI
vendors.sells: Makes head-worn cameras, puts them on factory workers through factory management, and publishes the first-person footage free under an open licence. No paid product, price list or customer is described on any page that could be read.

vendors.name: Cajal
vendors.sells: AI agents ("Tau") that write machine-checked mathematical proofs in Lean, pitched at quantum computing and finance; as a second line, proof datasets, evals and RL environments for frontier AI labs and research institutes.

vendors.name: Chakra Labs and Pango
vendors.sells: Pango (2025): a Chrome extension paying people to work in Sheets, Slides, Figma and Canva while recording screen and inputs. Chakra Labs (2026): exact clones of real software as environments, with tasks, graders, evals and datasets.

vendors.name: China robot-data market (cross-vendor notes)
vendors.sells: Market notes on robot data in China: hourly prices, industry capacity and funding of independent data firms.

vendors.name: Cortex AI
vendors.sells: First-person workplace video with hand and body pose, depth and sub-task labels; robot trajectories collected in real workplaces; remote operators who rescue deployed robots, with the rescue recorded. Plus a marketplace paying workplaces to host sessions.

vendors.name: CuriosityStream
vendors.sells: Rights to video it owns or has licensed in from other studios, packaged as labelled custom and off-the-shelf datasets for AI training; also audio and a private store of software code.

vendors.name: Datacurve
vendors.sells: Coding-centred training data and tests made by paid software engineers: RL environments, long tasks, recorded expert work sessions, worked examples for fine-tuning, ready-made datasets and benchmarks (DeepSWE). Contributors come through Shipd, a bounty site.

vendors.name: Datoric
vendors.sells: Recordings made to order by paid contributors through private invite-only apps, plus ready-made sets: robot and first-person video, computer-use traces, speech in many languages, two-person conversation, gameplay with inputs, voice-preference rankings.

vendors.name: David AI
vendors.sells: Recorded human speech licensed as datasets: two-speaker channel-separated conversation (Converse), multilingual (Atlas), three-plus speakers (Chorus), expert dialogue (Dialog); also voice-acting recordings, transcription and, new in 2026, evaluations of voice models. Contributors paid through Babel Audio.

vendors.name: Deeptune
vendors.sells: "Training gyms": simulated copies of workplace software (spreadsheets, Slack, Salesforce, ticketing, finance and monitoring tools) with tasks, data and infrastructure, where an agent practises and is scored. Sold to frontier research labs.

vendors.name: Defined.ai
vendors.sells: A marketplace of ready-made licensed datasets (speech, text, image, video, multimodal), some its own and many from outside data partners who earn licence fees; plus custom collection, annotation and evaluation using a paid crowd.

vendors.name: Defined.ai (audio pass)
vendors.sells: A marketplace of ready-made training datasets (its own and third parties'), plus made-to-order collection and annotation. Began as a speech-data company; now sells text, voice and image data.

vendors.name: Dyna
vendors.sells: Robot-model builder. Pre-trains on human first-person video, then a little robot data per task; runs its own operation and deployed robots; also takes video from data partners.

vendors.name: Encord (physical-AI line)
vendors.sells: A data platform (store, search, label and review video, depth, lidar, robot logs) plus a collection service: on-robot collection, teleoperation in Bay Area pods, first-person human video, hand-held gripper capture, action labelling and remote rescue of deployed robots.

vendors.name: Epoch AI
vendors.sells: Donor-funded nonprofit that also takes paid commissions: benchmark development (FrontierMath), model evaluation and analysis, custom research reports, data collection, data-centre intelligence, briefings, and an "Epoch on demand" retainer.

vendors.name: Figure
vendors.sells: Robot-model builder. Trains on its own crowd video and on internet video; collects through its own app and collectors in sensor suits; says it stopped buying from vendors.

vendors.name: Firstsource
vendors.sells: A labour pool ("Gigsourcing Platform") pointed at robot data: first-person video collection in homes with touch and body-position streams, teleoperation data pipelines, matched first- and third-person video, and defect image labelling.

vendors.name: Fleet AI
vendors.sells: Simulated software environments ("training gyms") where an AI agent attempts a real job task and gets graded; plus tasks, graders, benchmarks, post-training recipes and monitoring of agent behaviour. Sold to frontier labs, hyperscalers and enterprises.

vendors.name: General Intuition and Medal
vendors.sells: Medal, a free app, records gameplay clips with player inputs. General Intuition trains action and world models on the clips and sells model access through an API to partners in games, simulation and robotics. It sells no data.

vendors.name: Generalist
vendors.sells: Robot-model builder. Pre-trains on human-wearable data with no robot data, then a little robot data per task; ships its own wearables; says it has several data foundry partners; named as a customer by Scale AI.

vendors.name: Genesis AI
vendors.sells: buyer — trains on glove data, first-person video and internet video (no hours); collects with its own tactile glove on partners' workers; 'could also pay third-party partners' (TechCrunch).

vendors.name: Ginkgo Datapoints
vendors.sells: Fee-for-service lab data generation by robots, customer keeps the result: antibody developability, perturbation response profiling (DRUG-seq RNA and Cell Painting imaging), specialised high-throughput screens, small-molecule ADME.

vendors.name: Google DeepMind
vendors.sells: Robot-model builder. Collects its own two-arm teleoperation on its own fleet; Apptronik collects humanoid data for its robotics models.

vendors.name: Gradient Health
vendors.sells: "Atlas", a searchable library of de-identified medical scans with radiology reports, licensed to medical AI companies; from June 2026 adding health records, pathology, lab results and heart tracings. Also licenses through broker Protege.

vendors.name: Halluminate
vendors.sells: RL environments ("gyms") for finance knowledge work: a simulated desktop with data room, email, chat, spreadsheets and documents; expert-written tasks; graders; plus benchmarks showing where models fail. Sold to frontier AI labs.

vendors.name: Handshake AI
vendors.sells: Hourly expert contractors ("fellows") writing prompts, grading model answers, red-teaming and building tasks for AI labs; de-identified company records bought from companies and passed to labs; agent building and tuning for enterprises.

vendors.name: hillclimb
vendors.sells: RL environments and evals for AI-research ability, sold to frontier labs. At launch (Nov 2025): maths training data and maths RL environments written by elite mathematicians.

vendors.name: HUD
vendors.sells: An open-source SDK for defining RL environments, tasks and graders; a hosted platform that runs agents against them, records traces and can train on results; and "DataVendor", a marketplace where outside builders sell environments and training data to labs.

vendors.name: Human Archive (YC W26)
vendors.sells: Two datasets collected mostly through Indian home-service, hotel and restaurant firms whose staff wear its kit: HA-Multi (depth video, tactile gloves, body motion sensors, wrist cameras, time-aligned) and HA-Ego (single-camera video with labels); also robot-deployment, image and audio sets.

vendors.name: Human Native (now part of Cloudflare)
vendors.sells: Before the deal: a UK marketplace turning publishers' and creators' content into licensed, structured datasets for AI developers. Cloudflare has since shipped Pay Per Use, Pay Per Crawl and AI Index for paid, metered AI access to publisher content.

vendors.name: Illumina BioInsight / Billion Cell Atlas
vendors.sells: Membership of an alliance with access to a very large single-cell dataset of genetic perturbations that Illumina is generating, hosted on its own cloud.

vendors.name: Invisible Technologies
vendors.sells: To model builders: RL environments, agent and tool-use training, custom evaluations, off-the-shelf datasets, multimodal and multilingual data, SFT demonstrations, RLHF comparisons and red-teaming, staffed by experts from its Meridial marketplace. To enterprises: forward-deployed engineers, platform and staffing.

vendors.name: Irregular (formerly Pattern Labs)
vendors.sells: Pre-release tests of how well a new AI model can hack: it builds targets (simulated networks, real phones, routers, databases, software), runs the model against them and reports scores. Also sells its SOLVE difficulty scoring, defence research and policy work.

vendors.name: Kled
vendors.sells: A phone app where ordinary people upload photos, video, voice and documents and do paid tasks; Kled filters for fraud, packages and licenses datasets to AI labs and enterprises. Also holds exclusive AI licences on TV, cartoon and drone archives.

vendors.name: Labelbox (and Alignerr)
vendors.sells: Horizon: RL environments and evaluations for frontier labs, authored and graded by its Alignerr contractor network. Terra: robotics data recorded on Labelbox-supplied rigs. Recursion: managed, graded agents for enterprises. Legacy annotation software.

vendors.name: Lightwheel / 光轮智能
vendors.sells: Human first-person work recordings ("EgoSuite"); simulated assets and synthetic robot data ("AutoDataGen" on its "SimFoundry" physics solver); simulated robot-model testing ("RoboFinals"); and "RoboStack", feeding deployed-robot failures into the next data order.

vendors.name: Arena (formerly LMArena)
vendors.sells: A free public site where people vote between anonymous models, plus paid "AI Evaluations": labs and enterprises pay for evaluations on that community, pre-release testing under codenames, and the data behind results. Also an API/router, data products and AutoEval.

vendors.name: Luel
vendors.sells: A two-sided marketplace: contributors record audio, video and images by app, paid per accepted submission; AI teams order collections to a spec or license finished sets. Luel Labs also builds speech models and voices from the data.

vendors.name: Magma
vendors.sells: A broker: a company running an AI agent connects its database; Magma strips identifying details, packages the agent logs (actions, user corrections, finished jobs) into training environments and licenses them to AI labs, sharing each licence fee with the supplier.

vendors.name: Mantic
vendors.sells: Probability forecasts of real-world events for hedge funds and companies, with a tool to create and track personalised forecasts and MCP and API access, built on other labs' models. It pays people to write hard forecasting questions.

vendors.name: Markov
vendors.sells: Recordings of professionals using desktop software with time-aligned mouse and keyboard events and narration: "CAD environments" (problem statement, reference inputs, gold output file, grading rubric) and plain supervised-training recordings for browser, coding, design and spreadsheet work.

vendors.name: Mechanize
vendors.sells: Hand-built software-engineering tasks, each a prompt plus a sandbox plus an automatic grader, bundled into environments that frontier labs use for RL training or evaluation; one salaried engineer per task, about one task a week.

vendors.name: Mecka AI
vendors.sells: Calibrated multi-sensor first-person capture of people doing real work on its own hardware (body sensors, tactile gloves, camera rigs, phones), reconstructed into motion and geometry; bespoke programmes for labs; a capture app, dataset browser and programming interfaces; robot deployment as integrator.

vendors.name: Medra
vendors.sells: Robots plus AI that run wet-lab experiments, installed at the customer or run in its own lab; for model builders, experimental biology data on demand.

vendors.name: Mercor
vendors.sells: Vetted expert labour for labs (tasks, rubrics, grading); RL environments; off-the-shelf licensed datasets; APEX benchmarks and post-training research; company data licensing (Slack, email, CRM, code, documents) and wearable-camera robotics video; enterprise AI builds and evals.

vendors.name: METR
vendors.sells: Not a seller: a donor-funded research nonprofit producing capability scores (time horizon), pre-release evaluations of unreleased models, and embedded risk assessments inside labs (monitor red-teaming, incident investigation, risk-report reviews).

vendors.name: micro1
vendors.sells: Realm: evaluations and RL environments for AI labs built by contracted experts; Cortex: agent evaluation and monitoring for enterprises; Robotics: filmed demonstrations, annotation, a robot lab; a government line; buys company operating data to build RL environments.

vendors.name: micro1 — robotics department
vendors.sells: Labour-and-data service for robot labs: paid-crowd first-person home and workplace video with phone motion data, expert-demonstrated capture, annotation of robot and human video, on-site US teleoperation in shifts, and a Malibu lab that runs, records and evaluates robots.

vendors.name: microAGI (microagi GmbH) — Shift and Atlas
vendors.sells: Shift: pays workers to film their own work first-person on a head-strapped phone and sells the lightly labelled footage to robot-model labs. Atlas: records factory workers, fine-tunes a partner's robot model, installs a partner's robot, rented on success. Post-training research.

vendors.name: MiFeng / 觅蜂科技 (AgiBot spin-out)
vendors.sells: Capture kits (a head unit with several cameras, wrist cameras, a hand-held gripper); robot teleoperation, simulation and robot-free human capture data, stock first then to order; processing software; a gig collection app; sold as a licence or outright.

vendors.name: Moonlake
vendors.sells: buyer — world-model builder; trains on two-arm robot logs replayed through its simulator (no hours); hiring to 'collect and curate real-world robotics datasets'; uses data in the format of XDOF's open set.

vendors.name: Moonvalley / Asteria (now part of Reka)
vendors.sells: Marey, a text-to-video and image-to-video model for film and advertising trained only on licensed footage; it pays for footage and runs an annotator platform. Since June 2026 the team is at Reka, whose Claru line sells egocentric, robot data.

vendors.name: NVIDIA (GR00T, EgoScale)
vendors.sells: Robot-model builder. Trained on human first-person video and a small amount of its own teleoperation, multiplied by video generation; publishes open datasets.

vendors.name: Ocular AI
vendors.sells: Studio-quality recordings of real conversation with each speaker on a separate channel, evaluations that show where a voice model fails, matched audio-plus-video recordings, and an Expert Network of paid contributors.

vendors.name: Origin Lab
vendors.sells: Licensed gameplay video recorded inside the game engine by paid players, with keyboard and mouse inputs, depth, surface normals, audio, camera telemetry and game state on one clock; sold to world-model and video-generation labs via API.

vendors.name: Outlier (Scale AI's contractor brand)
vendors.sells: Scale AI's contributor marketplace: paid freelance tasks (hard prompts, grading rubrics, rating and ranking model answers, voice conversations, image/video comparison, phone-screen recordings with an AI assistant) — the labour behind Scale's Gen AI data business.

vendors.name: Petrarch
vendors.sells: Broker of private company records: finds companies with unused internal data (including bankrupt ones), checks ownership, strips personal information on the supplier's machines (Lindo), restructures it, and resells to applied AI startups and labs.

vendors.name: Phinity Labs
vendors.sells: Markets autonomous chip design; revenue today is work for AI model labs: RL environments, graders, agent infrastructure and evaluation for hardware (chip-design) tasks, including benchmarking unreleased models.

vendors.name: Physical Intelligence
vendors.sells: Robot-model builder. Trains on data from many robots, autonomous runs, human first-person video, open sets and web data; collects by teleoperation in shifts; named as a customer by Scale AI.

vendors.name: Plato
vendors.sells: Simulated copies of real web and desktop software (replica sites, VM images of business apps, an Ubuntu desktop) that agents act in and are scored on, plus a pipeline turning customers' real traces into environments; for browser and computer-use agents.

vendors.name: Preference Model
vendors.sells: RL environments (task plus sandbox plus grader) for one domain: the work of an ML engineer or researcher — kernel writing, post-training, data curation, experiment design — delivered into buyers' training runs. Gives away Karotte, an open-source framework.

vendors.name: Prime Intellect
vendors.sells: Not a human-data vendor: machinery for RL training — Environments Hub and open-source verifiers library, hosted training and evaluations (Lab), sandboxes, inference and rented GPU clusters; runs an open hub of community environments.

vendors.name: Protege
vendors.sells: Broker of licensed, non-public real-world data: signs data owners (hospitals, labs, broadcasters, sports bodies, game and scanning companies), curates and delivers datasets to AI developers, pays owners per use; also builds evaluation sets and benchmarks, healthcare first.

vendors.name: Protege — audio and speech side
vendors.sells: Audio that already exists in the world, licensed from the organisations that hold it, then filtered and quality-checked for training (clinical, call-centre, courtroom, Indic, Arabic, low-resource languages; human-reviewed transcripts). Does not record to order.

vendors.name: Protege — video licensing arm (Protege Media)
vendors.sells: Licensed video from broadcasters, studios, sports rights holders and platforms under revenue-share deals with exclusive AI-training rights, pooled in one store and built into clipped, filtered, face-masked, rights-checked datasets when a lab orders.

vendors.name: Proximal
vendors.sells: Hard, long-running coding tasks packaged as RL environments (task, sandbox, grader), evaluations showing where a model is weak, and post-training data aimed at the weakness; also post-trains open models itself to prove the data works.

vendors.name: Scale AI
vendors.sells: Human-made training and evaluation data for model builders (SFT, preference data, rubrics, red-teaming, RL environments, coding and agent evaluations, robotics demonstrations), public benchmarks, enterprise and government agent applications, and since 2026 buying companies' operating records to build RL environments.

vendors.name: Scale AI — physical-AI line
vendors.sells: Teleoperated two-arm demonstrations from its own cells, a robot-free wearable rig, collection on the customer's hardware, annotation and expert review, ready-made datasets tested by fine-tuning a policy, recording software in Universal Robots' AI Trainer, a planned robot-data marketplace.

vendors.name: SimpleClosure AssetHub
vendors.sells: Winds down startups; AssetHub takes their code and internal records (SourceCode: repositories, tickets, docs; WorkspaceData: Slack, email, Drive, Notion, Figma), strips personal data, and sells or licenses them to AI buyers. Since Sep 2026 also takes operating companies.

vendors.name: Skild
vendors.sells: Robot-model builder. Trains on human video, simulation, teleoperation and deployment logs; says it scales all collection in house.

vendors.name: Snorkel AI
vendors.sells: Finished datasets, benchmarks and RL environments built by paid domain experts plus Snorkel's own software and models, sold off-the-shelf (Snorkel Data Series, quarterly releases) or custom; a second line builds specialized agents for enterprises and government.

vendors.name: Haitian Ruisheng / Speechocean (北京海天瑞声, 688787)
vendors.sells: Training datasets sold two ways: ready-made datasets it owns and licenses repeatedly, and made-to-order collection and labelling, across speech, computer vision and text; a new application-services line (digital humans, voice-model platforms, government data platforms).

vendors.name: Surge AI
vendors.sells: Human-made training and test data for AI labs (practice environments, rubrics and verifiers, demonstrations, human evaluation, expert fields, many languages, several media); now also ready-made datasets sold with before-and-after benchmark scores, and a service that evaluates, improves and trains models for enterprises.

vendors.name: Tahoe Therapeutics
vendors.sells: Large single-cell datasets showing how cells respond to drugs, made in its own lab with the Mosaic method (many cell lines pooled and treated together); also builds its own models and drug programmes on the same data.

vendors.name: Tempus AI
vendors.sells: Licences to de-identified patient data from its own cancer testing labs (DNA/RNA sequencing, pathology images, clinical notes), plus analysis and, increasingly, a place to train models on that data with GPUs attached; licensed to drug companies.

vendors.name: Theta (Theta Software Inc.)
vendors.sells: Custom RL environments for professional knowledge work (finance, back office, healthcare, legal, IT, software), built from a customer's own data plus Theta's hired experts; and the trained or tuned agents that come out of them, delivered hands-on.

vendors.name: Toloka (and its contributor brand Mindrift)
vendors.sells: To labs: human-made training and test data, RL gyms (simulated companies and apps), off-the-shelf datasets, red-teaming, robotics video. To enterprises: fine-tuning service, private leaderboard (Arena), labelling platform. Tendem: vetted humans callable by agents. Workers recruited through Mindrift.

vendors.name: Troveo
vendors.sells: Broker of licensed, non-public media: signs content owners (creators, broadcasters, sports bodies, game and esports companies), indexes, labels and delivers footage to AI developers. Since Apr 2026 also audio, text, enterprise workflow data, gaming, robotics data; company records; custom sourcing.

vendors.name: Turing
vendors.sells: To labs: training datasets, RL environments and benchmarks in software engineering, enterprise knowledge work and advanced STEM; off-the-shelf data packs; Turing Frontier expert network; Project Lazarus, which buys companies' internal records. To enterprises: forward-deployed engineers building agent systems.

vendors.name: Vals AI
vendors.sells: A testing firm, not a data vendor: independent benchmark runs on private test sets published as leaderboards, pre-release testing for labs, private validation sets licensed to companies, Vals Smith (a company's GitHub repository turned into a coding benchmark), government evaluation.

vendors.name: Vision Lab (YC)
vendors.sells: First-person video from live factory lines, paired with a wider fixed view of the station and the written procedure (which step, what order, which tool, done right or wrong); also trains its own model to read factory video.

vendors.name: Wirestock
vendors.sells: Photos, video, design files and three-dimensional assets made by freelance creators, sold to AI labs as training data: an off-the-shelf library and custom jobs where creators shoot or edit to a lab's brief and Wirestock labels and checks.

vendors.name: World-model builders (general notes)
vendors.sells: World-model builders as a class: they license gameplay video with controls, and Chinese vendors count them as buyers of robot-free human data.

vendors.name: XDOF
vendors.sells: Robot demonstrations made by people driving robots: teleoperation on the buyer's own robot, teleoperation on its standard two-arm rigs, and first-person human data from sensor-wearing collectors; plus cleaning, annotation, a dataset portal (Foundry), policy-training support and evaluation.
